---
title: What is ivue?
description: 'ivue builds Vue 3 reactivity from plain TypeScript classes. One kilobyte, zero dependencies, native inheritance. Meet Reactive(), the v2 engine.'
---

# What is ivue?

**ivue** (Infinite Vue) builds Vue 3 reactivity out of plain TypeScript
classes. Real inheritance. Real encapsulation. Real polymorphism. The whole
engine is **1,052 bytes gzipped** with zero dependencies.

`Reactive()` transforms a class's prototype **once**:

- **getters** that return `ref()` / `computed()` become lazily cached reactive cells,
- **methods** become lazily bound functions,

and instances stay **ordinary objects**. No `reactive()` proxy wraps them. No
work happens at construction.

```ts
import { Reactive } from 'ivue'
import { ref, computed } from 'vue'

class $Timer {
  get seconds() { return ref(0) }
  get label() { return computed(() => `${this.seconds.value}s`) }
  tick() { this.seconds.value++ }
}
export const Timer = Reactive($Timer)
```

```ts
const t = new Timer()
t.tick()
t.seconds.value // 1
t.label.value   // "1s"
```

## Why classes?

Composables are great for small, local state. Growing apps want **structure**:
shared base behavior, overridable pieces, encapsulated internals, a clear
"this is the model" boundary. Classes give you that natively. `extends`,
`super`, `private`, getters and setters. ivue makes them reactive without
taking any of it away.

And classes host composables, not replace them:

```ts
class $Pointer {
  get $mouse() { return useMouse() }   // a composable, created once per instance
  get x() { return this.$mouse.x }
}
```

## ivue v1 vs v2

ivue ships two engines. They express the same idea differently.

| | **v1 — `ivue()`** | **v2 — `Reactive()`** |
|---|---|---|
| How | wraps each instance in Vue `reactive()` | transforms the prototype once; instances stay plain |
| State | fields via `iref()`, no `.value` | getters return `ref()`, read with `.value` |
| Creation | a proxy + eager computeds per instance | a bare `new`; state is lazy |
| Memory | per-instance computeds | derivations shared on the prototype, up to **18.6× lighter** |
| Modules | hierarchy in one file (HMR) | cross-file hierarchies, circular-import immunity |
| Extras | `.clone()`, `.toRefs()`, `init()` | lean core: `$watch`, `$stopEffects` |

::: tip Which should I use?
**v2** for everything new, and for anything with many instances or deep
structure. **v1** where you rely on `.clone()` / `.toRefs()` today. The
[migration](/guide/migration) is smaller than it looks: only mutable state
converts.
:::

## The trade, in one line

v2 is **cheap to create and light to hold, slightly costlier to read**: state
sits behind a getter, so hot loops pay ~5× per read over a raw closure ref.
One [hoist line](/guide/performance#hot-loops) erases it. Everything else is
free.

Next: the [principles](/guide/principles) that make it work.

## Derived values: plain getters first

Derive with a **plain getter** by default. No `computed()`:

```ts
class $Box {
  get w() { return ref(4) }
  get h() { return ref(3) }
  get area() { return this.w.value * this.h.value } // plain getter
}
```

It stays fully reactive: whatever effect reads `area` — a render, a watcher —
reads `w` and `h` underneath and subscribes to them directly. Change a source
and the effect re-runs.

Why this is the default:

- **Zero memory per instance.** A plain getter lives once, on the prototype.
  Every `computed()` allocates ~300 bytes per instance, paid at creation,
  read or not. Sixty computeds on 10k instances is real megabytes — see
  [Memory](/guide/performance#memory-derivations-weigh-nothing).
- **Zero staleness.** The value re-derives whenever it's read. Nothing to
  invalidate, nothing to reason about.
- **The engine helps.** On first access it sees a non-ref result and restores
  a native prototype getter — from then on it's ordinary JavaScript.

<DemoState />

## computed(): the surgical opt-in

Wrap a getter in `computed()` when the memoization earns its bytes:

```ts
get sorted() {
  return computed(() => [...this.rows.value].sort(byScore)) // expensive: memoize
}
```

Reach for it when:

- the derivation is genuinely **expensive** (sorting/filtering large arrays);
- an unchanged result should **suppress re-renders** (Vue 3.4+ computeds stop
  propagation on equal values, plain getters cannot);
- you need a **stable ref identity** to hand to `watch`, a prop, or a composable.

Read it with `.value` — standard Vue computed semantics.

## Derived values: plain getters by default

The most important thing on this page: **you usually don't need `computed()`.**
A plain getter is already reactive.

```ts
class $Cart {
  get items() { return ref<{ price: number }[]>([]) }
  get total() { return this.items.value.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price, 0) }
}
```

When a render (or watcher) reads `total`, execution runs synchronously inside
that effect — so every reactive leaf the getter touches subscribes the effect
directly. A source changes, the effect re-runs, the getter re-derives.
Dependencies re-collect on every run, so conditional branches always track
correctly.

The payoff is memory. A plain getter lives once on the prototype and weighs
**zero bytes per instance**. Every eager `computed()` costs ~300 bytes per
instance at creation, read or not — 60 of them on a 10k-row list is ~300 MB
of pure bookkeeping avoided. Full numbers in
[Memory](/guide/performance#memory-derivations-weigh-nothing).

## computed(): your useMemo

Wrap a getter in `computed()` when memoization earns its bytes:

- the derivation is genuinely **expensive** (sorting/filtering large arrays,
  heavy string building);
- an unchanged result should **suppress re-renders** — a Vue 3.4+ computed
  stops propagation when the value is equal, a plain getter cannot;
- you need a **stable ref identity** to hand to `watch`, a prop, or a
  composable.

```ts
get sorted() {
  return computed(() => [...this.items.value].sort(byPrice))
}
```

Each instance and each inheritance level caches its computed under a distinct
key, so overrides and `super` never collide
([Inheritance](/guide/inheritance)).

See both side by side — the plain getter re-derives freely while the
computed's body only runs when its dependency actually changes:

<DemoDerived />

<script setup lang="ts">
import { computed, onMounted, ref, watch } from 'vue';
import { Reactive } from '../../../../lib/Reactive';
import DemoBox from './DemoBox.vue';

// Plain (non-reactive) counter: incrementing it inside the computed body is
// side-effect-free for the graph. A post-flush watcher mirrors it into a ref.
let runs = 0;
const statusRuns = ref(0);

class $Thermo {
  get celsius() {
    return ref(21);
  }
  // Plain getter: re-derives every render. Perfect for trivial math.
  get fahrenheit() {
    return Math.round((this.celsius.value * 9) / 5 + 32);
  }
  // computed(): memoized. Reach for it when the work is real.
  get status() {
    return computed(() => {
      runs++;
      const c = this.celsius.value;
      if (c < 10) return 'Cold';
      if (c < 18) return 'Cool';
      if (c < 26) return 'Comfortable';
      return 'Warm';
    });
  }
}
const Thermo = Reactive($Thermo);
const t: any = new Thermo();

onMounted(() => {
  statusRuns.value = runs;
  watch(
    () => t.celsius.value,
    () => {
      statusRuns.value = runs;
    },
    { flush: 'post' },
  );
});
</script>

All three asks shipped — committed `21ba371`, live at **http://10.0.0.1:5174/**.

## 1. Hero honesty fix
The demo card no longer claims `$watch` — the component now uses **plain Vue `watch`** and the log line is labeled `watch`, matching reality. And went further: the hero's `double` is now a **plain getter** in both the displayed code and the running class, labeled *"double (plain getter)"* — so the hero now demonstrates your derive-on-render doctrine instead of contradicting it.

## 2. Plain-getter doctrine, everywhere
Your migration.md insight — *simple derivations don't need `computed()`; plain getters are reactive via derive-on-render and prevent per-instance memory accumulation* — is now the consistent teaching across the funnel:

- **Home** — code sample: `get double() { return this.count.value * 2 }` with *"computed() is opt-in"*.
- **Introduction** — transform bullets now name plain derived getters as a first-class mode; Timer example converted.
- **Getting Started** — first class uses a plain getter, with a "note what double is *not*" callout.
- **State** — new sections: *"Derived values: plain getters first"* (zero bytes/instance vs ~300 B per eager computed, zero staleness, engine de-opt) and *"computed(): the surgical opt-in"* (your three criteria).
- **Computed & Watch** — rewritten around the doctrine; *"computed(): your useMemo"*.
- **Principles** — #4 reframed from "self-optimizing" to *"Derive with plain getters; the engine self-optimizes"*.
- **API + Invariants** — de-optimization now documented as the mechanism behind the recommended authoring mode, not just an escape hatch.

## 3. Live demos on every core page
Six components, all importing the **real engine from `lib/Reactive.ts`**, sharing a `DemoBox` shell that matches the hero card, each badged *"Live · runs the shipped engine"*:

| Page | Demo |
|---|---|
| Getting Started | the exact class from the tutorial, running |
| Reactive State | sliders → refs, plain-getter `area` deriving live |
| Computed & Watch | **plain getter vs `computed()` side by side** — with a body-run counter proving the memoization |
| Inheritance | 3-level `super` chain; mutate a grandparent ref, watch the chain recompute |
| Teardown | full `$watch`/`$stopEffects` lifecycle (the one place `$watch` belongs) |
| Performance | **"Create 100,000 instances"** benchmark visitors run in their own browser, with live ratios |

**All verified by driving them in jsdom** — clicks, sliders, watch fires, dispose stops, benchmark produces ratios. One bug caught and fixed in the process: my first run-counter wrote a ref inside the computed body, which caused a recursive-update error; replaced with a plain counter mirrored by a post-flush watcher, re-verified clean.

The docs now don't just describe the engine — every core page proves it in front of the reader.

1	# Formula grid — 100,000 live cells with real Excel formulas
2	
3	A working spreadsheet where cells hold **real Excel-formula syntax**
4	(`=A1+B2`, `=SUM(A1:D1)`, `=IF(A1>0,B1,C1)`), parsed and evaluated by the real
5	[`fast-formula-parser`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/fast-formula-parser) npm
6	package (not a stub — it bundles 280 Excel-compatible functions), wired so that
7	**Vue's own reactivity discovers each formula's dependencies automatically** —
8	there is no hand-built dependency graph anywhere in this demo.
9	
10	This is the `demo/grid` benchmark's architecture (virtualization, row-windowing,
11	the create/scroll/edit verification pattern, the gc-forced 3-run heap protocol)
12	with the toy string-concat `IvueCell` replaced by a real `FormulaCell` that
13	parses and evaluates. The point is to measure the **honest** heap cost of doing
14	that at 100k cells, and to prove the reactivity claims end-to-end.
15	
16	## The integration seam (how Vue discovers the graph)
17	
18	Three files, following the ivue operating manual exactly:
19	
20	- **`FormulaCell.ts`** — a `Reactive()` class, same shape as `demo/grid`'s
21	  `IvueCell`:
22	  - `raw` → a **ref-getter** holding the literal text the user typed (`"42"`,
23	    `"hello"`, or `"=A1+B2"`).
24	  - `value` → the **one** `computed()` (the hot, correctly-memoized value:
25	    parsing + evaluating a formula is real work). If `raw` isn't a formula it
26	    resolves the literal; if it is, it calls `sheet.evaluate(this, body)`.
27	  - `display` / `isFormula` / `cssClass` → **plain getters** (0 bytes/instance,
28	    reactive via leaf tracking).
29	- **`Sheet.ts`** — a plain (non-reactive) container holding the 100,000
30	  `FormulaCell` instances in a `grid[row][col]` that doubles as an O(1)
31	  `cellAt(row, col)`. It owns **one shared `FormulaParser`** (never one per
32	  cell) whose `onCell`/`onRange` hooks read cells' `value.value`.
33	- The seam: those `onCell`/`onRange` reads happen **while a cell's `value`
34	  computed is evaluating**, so Vue records them as that computed's dependencies.
35	  Edit a referenced cell and every dependent formula invalidates and
36	  recomputes — cascading through the graph — with **no manual re-render call**.
37	
38	The parser needs a shared singleton because a per-cell parser would reintroduce
39	exactly the per-instance allocation this whole line of work fights. It's built
40	once, in the `Sheet` constructor, and closes over `this` so its hooks resolve
41	through that sheet's `cellAt`.
42	
43	## Machine
44	
45	- Parallels VM, **aarch64** (Apple-silicon host), 16 vCPU, 31 GiB RAM
46	- Linux 6.8.0-134-generic
47	- Node v26.3.1 · Vue 3.5.x · `fast-formula-parser` 1.0.19
48	- Playwright headless Chromium, launched with `--js-flags=--expose-gc` and
49	  `--enable-precise-memory-info`; heap read via
50	  `performance.memory.usedJSHeapSize`.
51	
52	## The 100k population — a REAL cross-cell dependency graph
53	
54	Not 100k independent trivial formulas. Of the 100,000 cells, **52,500 (52.5%)
55	are cross-referencing formulas** and the rest are the numeric source data they
56	read (`formula-logic.ts`, `initialFormula`):
57	
58	| cols | contents                                | kind                              |
59	| ---- | --------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
60	| A–D  | numeric input (some blanks/negatives)   | source data                       |
61	| E    | `=A+B`                                  | cross-cell arithmetic             |
62	| F    | `=C-D`                                  | cross-cell arithmetic             |
63	| G    | `=SUM(A:D)`                             | range → exercises `onRange`       |
64	| H    | `=AVERAGE(A:D)`                         | range → exercises `onRange`       |
65	| I    | `=IF(A>0, B, C)`                        | **conditional dependency**        |
66	| J    | `=J(r-1)+A`, reset every 50 rows        | **running sum** (marquee cascade) |
67	| K…AN | even col = d

… [4,683 characters removed from the sample] …

rying real formula text and
142	a real dependency graph, the ivue formula grid virtualizes to **8.4 MB** —
143	**~9× under** the idiomatic composable arm's 77.3 MB for the _toy_ cell, let
144	alone what a per-cell-parser or eager-computed formula model would cost.
145	
146	## Verification (all via Playwright against the live dev server)
147	
148	Every check below is asserted in `measure.mjs` run 1 and passed on every run.
149	
150	### Real formula evaluation is correct
151	
152	| cell | formula           |  result | check           |
153	| ---- | ----------------- | ------: | --------------- |
154	| E1   | `=A1+B1`          | −642.39 | = A1 + B1 ✓     |
155	| G1   | `=SUM(A1:D1)`     | −854.34 | = A1+B1+C1+D1 ✓ |
156	| H1   | `=AVERAGE(A1:D1)` | −213.58 | = SUM/4 ✓       |
157	| J2   | `=J1+A2`          |   (sum) | running sum ✓   |
158	
159	Text typed into a cell resolves as text; a bad reference or `1/0` yields the
160	real `#VALUE!` / `#DIV/0!` errors (rendered amber); `=` alone renders blank.
161	
162	### The conditional-dependency test — PASSED
163	
164	`I1 = =IF(A1>0, B1, C1)`. The dependency Vue tracks **shifts** as A1 crosses
165	zero — proven three ways:
166	
167	- **A1 = −5 (< 0):** I1's live tracked deps = **{A1, C1}** (no B1); I1 = 215.22
168	  (= C1). ✓
169	- **A1 = 5 (> 0):** deps **shift to {A1, B1}** (no C1); I1 = −142.39 (= B1). ✓
170	- **Behavioral** (with A1 > 0, so I1 depends on B1 not C1): editing the
171	  **off-branch** C1 to `424242` leaves I1 **unchanged** (−142.39); editing the
172	  **live-branch** B1 to `777` moves I1 to **777**. ✓
173	
174	The dep set is read by re-walking the exact same `onCell` path Vue tracks, so it
175	_is_ Vue's live dependency set — which is why editing an off-branch cell provably
176	doesn't touch the formula.
177	
178	### Cross-cell cascade, live in the DOM — PASSED
179	
180	Editing input `A101 = 100000` updated running-sum cell `J106` (five links down
181	the chain) from `206` to `100,266` in the **rendered DOM**, with no manual
182	re-render. Observed live in the browser: flipping `A1` from −500 to 5,000
183	cascaded E1, F/G/H1, I1 (flipped C1→B1), the entire J block, and cross-column L
184	— all at once — while the untouched data columns stayed put.
185	
186	## Caveats (honest notes)
187	
188	- **The heap delta includes ~viewport DOM** (~960 mounted cells), identical to
189	  the toy grid, so the arm-to-arm _difference_ is the model difference.
190	- **`shallowRef` for the model.** The `Sheet` is held in a `shallowRef`, so
191	  neither it, its `grid`, nor its 100k cells are ever deep-proxied; per-cell
192	  reactivity comes entirely from each cell's own ref/computed.
193	- **Creation includes parser build + formula-string generation.** `creationMs`
194	  covers building the one chevrotain-backed parser (a fixed one-time cost) and
195	  generating every cell's formula text, which is why it runs a few ms above the
196	  toy grid's construction. Neither cost is per-render.
197	- **Recursion guard.** A user-typed circular reference (`A1: =A1`) returns
198	  `#REF!` via a cheap per-evaluation guard rather than overflowing the stack; the
199	  guard allocates nothing per cell.
200	- Single-machine, single-browser (Chromium/V8) on aarch64; absolute bytes will
201	  differ elsewhere, but the ratios are the load-bearing result.
202	
203	## Reproduce
204	
205	```bash
206	# from the ivue repo root
207	npx yarn install                                   # fast-formula-parser is a devDependency
208	npx playwright install chromium                     # once
209	npx vite demo --host --port 5182                    # serve the demo (any free port)
210	node demo/formula/measure.mjs http://localhost:5182         # 100k cells (default)
211	node demo/formula/measure.mjs http://localhost:5182 25000   # 1M cells (25,000 rows)
212	```
213	
214	Then open `http://localhost:5182/grid-formula`, click **create model (100k)**,
215	click any cell to edit its formula, and watch dependents cascade.

1	---
2	title: Benchmarks
3	description: 'A live, in-browser 100k/1M-cell virtualized grid — the same model built three ways (composable, ivue, plain POJO) — plus the measured heap and creation-time numbers behind the claim.'
4	---
5	
6	# Benchmarks
7	
8	[The Reactive Model Layer](/guide/model-layer) argues that a domain model —
9	thousands of live, individually-reactive entities — has a structural memory
10	cost in idiomatic Vue, and that ivue's laziness erases it. This page is the
11	receipt: a real, reproducible, end-to-end measurement, not a microbenchmark.
12	[Performance](/guide/performance) covers the micro-level numbers (creation of
13	isolated instances, per-read cost); this page covers what happens when you
14	build an actual grid out of them.
15	
16	The same 40-column virtualized spreadsheet grid is built three ways from
17	identical seeded data:
18	
19	- **Composable** — the idiomatic Vue 3 "composable per entity": every cell
20	  eagerly allocates a `ref()` plus four `computed()`s.
21	- **ivue** — a `Reactive()` class `$Cell`: `raw` is a ref-getter, three
22	  derived values are **plain getters** (0 bytes/instance), and only the one
23	  hot value is a `computed()`. Refs/computeds materialize lazily.
24	- **POJO floor** — plain `{ row, col, raw }` objects, no reactivity at all.
25	  The theoretical memory minimum; edits don't re-render, by design.
26	
27	## Try it
28	
29	Click a button — it builds all three models at once, from the same data, so
30	every number below is directly comparable. Nothing runs until you click:
31	this is a live embed of the shipped engine, not a video.
32	
33	<GridBenchmark />
34	
35	## The measured numbers
36	
37	The live demo above is illustrative — same machine, same session, but not
38	gc-forced or run in isolation. The numbers below are the controlled
39	measurement: 3 runs per arm, median reported, headless Chromium, heap read
40	via `window.gc()` ×3 + `performance.memory.usedJSHeapSize`, one fresh page
41	load per arm. Full protocol, caveats and raw numbers in
42	[`demo/grid/RESULTS.md`](https://github.com/infinite-system/ivue/blob/main/demo/grid/RESULTS.md).
43	
44	### 100,000 cells (40 cols × 2,500 rows)
45	
46	| Arm        | Model heap (virtualized) | Bytes/cell | Model heap (all materialized) | Bytes/cell (mat.) |    Creation |
47	| ---------- | -----------------------: | ---------: | ----------------------------: | ----------------: | ----------: |
48	| Composable |                  77.3 MB |        773 |                      109.8 MB |             1,098 |     75.1 ms |
49	| **ivue**   |               **5.7 MB** |     **57** |                   **40.3 MB** |           **403** | **11.4 ms** |
50	| POJO floor |                   4.5 MB |         45 |                             — |                 — |     10.3 ms |
51	
52	### 1,000,000 cells (40 cols × 25,000 rows)
53	
54	| Arm        | Model heap (virtualized) | Bytes/cell | Model heap (all materialized) | Bytes/cell (mat.) |    Creation |
55	| ---------- | -----------------------: | ---------: | ----------------------------: | ----------------: | ----------: |
56	| Composable |                 757.7 MB |        758 |                    1,083.7 MB |             1,084 |    406.8 ms |
57	| **ivue**   |              **41.7 MB** |     **42** |                  **388.3 MB** |           **388** | **57.2 ms** |
58	| POJO floor |                  40.5 MB |         41 |                             — |                 — |     53.3 ms |
59	
60	### The sharpest number: marginal cost per added cell
61	
62	Scaling 100k → 1M (×10 cells) isolates the fixed viewport/DOM overhead from
63	the per-cell cost. The result:
64

## The formula grid: real formulas, discovered dependencies

The grids above prove the memory claim with a toy derivation. The formula
grid replaces the toy cell with a real one: a working spreadsheet whose cells
hold **actual Excel-formula syntax** — `=A1+B2`, `=SUM(A1:D1)`,
`=IF(A1>0,B1,C1)` — parsed and evaluated by the real
[`fast-formula-parser`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/fast-formula-parser)
package (280 Excel-compatible functions, not a stub).

The load-bearing fact: **there is no hand-built dependency graph anywhere.**
Each cell's `value` is the one `computed()`; the shared parser's
`onCell`/`onRange` hooks read referenced cells' `value.value` *while that
computed is evaluating*, so Vue records those reads as its dependencies. Edit
a cell and every dependent formula invalidates and recomputes, cascading
through the graph, with no manual invalidation call. This is the
[formula hole](/guide/model-layer) closed: the model stays at full size, at
the memory floor, and whole-range formulas just read through it.

And it is not 100k trivial formulas: **52.5% of the 100,000 cells are
cross-referencing formulas** — arithmetic, `SUM`/`AVERAGE` ranges,
conditionals, a 50-row running-sum cascade, a cross-column mesh.

### The numbers (3 runs, median, same protocol)

| Metric                        | Formula grid | Toy ivue grid |
| ----------------------------- | -----------: | ------------: |
| Model heap (virtualized)      |  **8.36 MB** |       5.70 MB |
| Bytes/cell (virtualized)      |           84 |            57 |
| Model heap (all materialized) |     48.11 MB |      40.30 MB |
| Creation time                 |      17.1 ms |       11.4 ms |
| Verification                  | **ALL PASS** |          pass |

**At 1M cells (virtualized):** 68.41 MB — **68 B/cell**, created in 104 ms,
with a marginal cost of ~67 B per added cell.

The +27 B/cell over the toy grid is accounted for, not hand-waved: the
formula **strings themselves** (52,500 formulas averaging ~13 chars are
simply longer than `-142.39` — real formulas are real bytes) and one `sheet`
back-pointer per cell. The materialized delta (+5.15 MB) is the **actual
dependency graph**: each formula computed subscribes to 1–4 other cells'
computeds — live cross-cell edges at ~100 B per formula cell. That is the
feature, priced honestly. Even carrying real formula text and a live
dependency graph, the formula grid virtualizes to **8.4 MB — still ~9× under
the composable arm's 77.3 MB for the toy cell**.

### What the verification proves

Every check runs in Playwright against the live DOM, asserted on every run:

- **Evaluation is correct** — `=SUM(A1:D1)`, `=AVERAGE(A1:D1)` and friends
  produce the arithmetic truth; bad references and `1/0` yield the real
  `#VALUE!` / `#DIV/0!` errors.
- **Conditional dependencies shift.** For `=IF(A1>0, B1, C1)`, the dependency
  set Vue tracks is `{A1, C1}` while A1 < 0 and **provably shifts** to
  `{A1, B1}` when A1 crosses zero — editing the off-branch cell leaves the
  formula untouched; editing the live branch moves it.
- **The cascade is live in the DOM.** Editing one input updated a running-sum
  cell five links down the chain in the rendered page, with no manual
  re-render.

Full write-up, machine notes, honest-cost accounting and caveats:
[`demo/formula/RESULTS.md`](https://github.com/infinite-system/ivue/blob/main/demo/formula/RESULTS.md).

```bash
node demo/formula/measure.mjs http://localhost:5182         # 100k protocol
node demo/formula/measure.mjs http://localhost:5182 25000   # 1M cells
```

## The formula grid is now a live docs embed

**`<FormulaGrid />`** sits in the Benchmarks page's formula section under "Try it" — same `DemoBox` pattern as every other live demo. What makes it more than a copy of the demo page:

- **Single source of truth** — it imports the *exact* `Sheet`/`FormulaCell` files from `demo/formula/` that produced the RESULTS.md numbers. No forked model in the docs.
- **The parser costs nothing until clicked** — `fast-formula-parser` arrives via dynamic import inside the click handler. Verified: VitePress SSR never executes it, and it ships as its own lazy chunk (`Sheet.*.js`), absent from the page's eager JS.
- **The conditional-dependency proof, made interactive** — the fx bar shows the selected cell's literal formula *plus its live tracked dependency set* (via `traceDeps`). A reader clicks I1, sees `reads: A1, C1`, sets A1 positive, re-selects — `reads: A1, B1`. The strongest claim in RESULTS.md is now something visitors do with their own hands.
- Create 100k or 1M, click-to-edit any cell, virtualized viewport, mounted-vs-model counter reinforcing the laziness story.

**Verified end-to-end in jsdom**: create 100k → E1 evaluates `A1+B1` → editing A1 through the UI cascades into the rendered DOM (`4,857.61`) → I1's dependency set shifts branches. All asserted.

- **A real environment bug**: npm had nested a second Vue runtime (3.5.24) under `@vue/test-utils` while everything else used the root 3.5.22 — two runtimes crashed slot rendering in *any* component test (`reading 'ce'`). Fixed durably in `vitest.config.ts` (dedupe vue + inline test-utils) rather than by node_modules surgery, so it survives future installs. Full suite green: **150 tests**.

Done — committed `2a78dd9`, live at **http://10.0.0.1:5174/** (server's running; scroll to "Hard problems, solved together").

## The moat redesign

**Design idea: the layout argues the claim.** The section's whole point is *"solved together, as one coherent design"* — so instead of 8 floating cards (which would visually say "eight separate things"), it's now a **fused monolith**: eight cells sharing 1px internal borders inside one rounded container, crowned by a single indigo→emerald gradient hairline running across the top. One physical block, one design.

Per cell: a CSS-drawn gradient **check badge** (no icon font, no SVG paths — border-rotation checkmark in the brand emerald), bold title, one-liner below, and a soft brand tint on hover. Collapses 4 → 2 → 1 columns.

**Verified with real eyes, not assumptions** — Playwright screenshots at desktop dark, desktop light, and 375px mobile: both themes hold (dividers legible in light, cells elevated in dark), no horizontal scroll, one-column collapse clean.

## Two content upgrades while in there

- **The hot-reload cell now claims what your engine actually does.** "The transform is idempotent" undersold your new class-HMR system — it now reads: *"Behavior edits graft onto live instances, state intact. Multi-file hierarchies never desync."* That's the stronger, true claim.
- **Start-here has its third card: Benchmarks** — "A 100k-cell grid built three ways, and a spreadsheet with real Excel formulas — live, in your browser. Run →". It's the natural third: the section directly above makes the moat claim, this card is its receipt. (The row was 2-of-3 after the migration card was retired with the "unreleased v1" reframe.) Plus a small arrow-slide on card hover.

**Bonus:** killed the `favicon.ico` 404 that fired on every page load — the SVG logo is now the favicon.

One note: the moat cells are static text, deliberately — the page already has the hero counter and links down to live proofs; making the moat cells clickable deep-links (each cell → its guide page) would be the next enhancement if you want it.

1	---
2	title: Principles
3	description: The seven guarantees behind ivue — plain instances, lazy cached state, self-optimizing getters, native inheritance, composable modules, and scoped teardown.
4	---
5	
6	# Principles
7	
8	Everything ivue does follows from a handful of guarantees. Knowing them is
9	enough to predict its behavior in any situation.
10	
11	## 1. Plain instances, no proxy
12	
13	`new Counter()` returns an ordinary object. `Reactive()` never wraps the instance
14	in `reactive()`. Reactivity comes only from the `ref()` / `computed()` you return
15	from getters — opt-in, per property.
16	
17	```ts
18	const c = new Counter()
19	isReactive(c) // false
20	```
21	
22	**Why it matters:** creating an instance costs a plain `new`. A million unused
23	instances cost almost nothing.
24	
25	## 2. State is a getter that returns a ref
26	
27	You declare reactive state as a getter returning `ref()`, `shallowRef()` or
28	`computed()`, and read/write through `.value`.
29	
30	```ts
31	get width() { return ref(100) }   // declaration
32	inst.width.value = 250            // read & write
33	```
34	
35	The getter body runs **at most once per instance** — the returned ref is cached
36	and reused on every later access, so the reactive identity is stable.
37	
38	## 3. Lazy + cached + stable
39	
40	Nothing is created until first access. After that it's cached on the instance:
41	
42	- a getter's ref/computed is created once, then returned identically every time;
43	- a method is bound once, then returned identically (referentially stable — safe
44	  as an event handler).
45	
46	## 4. Derive with plain getters; the engine self-optimizes
47	
48	Derived values are **plain getters by default**, not `computed()`:
49	
50	```ts
51	get area() { return this.w.value * this.h.value } // reactive, zero allocation
52	```
53	
54	On first access the engine sees a non-ref result and restores a native getter
55	on the prototype — from then on it is ordinary JavaScript, re-derived inside
56	whatever effect reads it. Plain getters live once on the prototype and weigh
57	**nothing per instance**; every eager `computed()` costs ~300 bytes per
58	instance whether it is ever read or not. Memoize surgically —
59	[when it earns it](/guide/computed-watch#computed-your-usememo).
60	
61	## 5. Native inheritance & `super`
62	
63	Processing runs base → child, and every `(prototype, key)` gets its own cache
64	symbol. So a child's computed and the `super` computed it calls cache separately
65	and never collide — `super.x.value` resolves through the whole chain exactly like
66	native classes. See [Inheritance](/guide/inheritance).
67	
68	## 6. Modules compose; circular references resolve
69	
70	Each class is transformed in its own file at load time, and the transform is
71	idempotent — shared ancestors are processed once, no matter the import order. The
72	[namespace pattern](/guide/modules) (`$Class` raw + `Class` reactive) exposes
73	classes through a hoisted object, so mutual cross-references between files resolve
74	in any order and survive cross-file HMR.
75	
76	## 7. Teardown is scope-based
77	
78	`$watch` registers watchers in a **lazily-created** per-instance effect scope;
79	`$stopEffects` stops that scope, runs an optional `stopEffects()` hook, and clears
80	the caches. Instances that never `$watch` allocate no scope — teardown stays
81	pay-for-what-you-use. See [Teardown](/guide/teardown).
82	
83	---
84	
85	::: info Want the formal version?
86	These are the user-facing form of the engine's invariants. For the rigorous
87	specification — mechanism, guarantees, and what each one makes *impossible* — see
88	[Invariants](/reference/invariants).
89	:::

1	---
2	title: Performance
3	description: The honest numbers. ivue creates instances 55–253× faster, uses up to 18× less memory per instance, and reads state ~5× slower in hot loops — a cost you can erase with a one-line hoist.
4	---
5	
6	# Performance
7	
8	ivue's design is one trade: **defer everything**. No proxy. No eager refs. No
9	binding until first access. Creation becomes extremely cheap. Reads pay a
10	small cost.
11	
12	## Creation is nearly free
13	
14	Creating an instance is a plain `new`. Refs and computeds do not exist until
15	you touch them. Measured on one machine:
16	
17	| creating 100k instances    | time       | ivue is         |
18	| -------------------------- | ---------- | --------------- |
19	| **ivue `new Class()`**     | **0.7 ms** | —               |
20	| native `reactive(new X())` | 36.7 ms    | **55× faster**  |
21	| native composable factory  | 42.8 ms    | **64× faster**  |
22	| v1 `ivue(Class)`           | 169 ms     | **253× faster** |
23	
24	ivue scales linearly at 10M instances: ~50 ms to allocate, ~1 s to also
25	materialize a ref and a computed on each, ~2.9 s for full **four-level**
26	hierarchies (40M+ Refs/Computeds). Unused instances cost almost nothing. This is ideal
27	for large lists and virtual scrolling.
28	
29	Don't take the table's word for it — run it on your own machine:
30	
31	<DemoPerf />
32	
33	::: info The embed measures production semantics
34	This page runs on a dev server, where ivue's [class HMR](/guide/hmr) arms a
35	construct-trap proxy that costs ~11× on bare instantiation (0.6 ms → 6.7 ms
36	per 100k — dev only; production bundles contain zero HMR code, verified by
37	grepping `dist/`). The docs opt out via
38	`globalThis[Symbol.for('ivue.hmr.disable')]` so the numbers you measure here
39	are the numbers production pays.
40	:::
41	
42	## Memory: derivations weigh nothing
43	
44	Every eager `computed()` costs real bytes **per instance**. You pay for the
45	`ComputedRefImpl`, its dependency links, and the closure. You pay even when
46	all it memoizes is trivial math.
47	
48	ivue stores derivations once, on the prototype, as plain getters. An instance
49	holds only the Refs it has actually materialized.
50	
51	Measured on Vue 3.5 with an identical shape — 10 state refs, 60 trivial
52	derivations, one full read pass, 20k instances:
53	
54	| authoring style                    | heap per instance | ivue is           |
55	| ---------------------------------- | ----------------- | ----------------- |
56	| **ivue class — 60 plain getters**  | **1.7 KB**        | —                 |
57	| composable — 60 plain closures     | 12.8 KB           | **7.7× lighter**  |
58	| composable — 60 eager `computed()` | 31.1 KB           | **18.6× lighter** |
59	
60	A trivial computed costs ≈300 bytes per instance. A closure costs ≈190. Both
61	are paid at creation, whether the value is ever read or not.
62	
63	The middle row is the sharp one. Skipping `computed()` inside a composable
64	still costs 7.7×, because **closures allocate per instance**. Only prototype
65	getters are shared. Skipping memoization is a policy win. The prototype is
66	the structural win. ivue stacks both by default.
67	
68	Scaled up: a 1,000-row grid of these components drops from ~31 MB to ~1.7 MB
69	of Refs/Computeds. For 10k virtualized items: ~311 MB → ~17 MB. The GC
70	pressure of creation bursts shrinks with it.
71	
72	This doesn't matter everywhere. A singleton store with 60 computeds costs
73	31 KB, total. And in many components, vnodes and DOM dominate the heap, not
74	Refs/Computeds. Use [`computed()`](/guide/computed-watch) where memoization
75	or render suppression earns its ~300 bytes.
76	
77	The same rule extends to the computeds you _do_ cache: point them at
78	methods — `computed(() => this.recalc())` — instead of inlining the logic.
79	The per-instance closure is then a pointer-sized hop to code that exists
80	once per class on the prototype, and it can never accidentally capture
81	getter-scope locals that would otherwise live as long as the instance —
82	the guaranteed-minimum footprint
83	([the thin convention](/guide/computed-watch#point-the-computed-at-a-method)),
84	and the shape that hot-reloads onto live instances ([HMR](/guide/hmr)).
85	
86	## The whole engine is ~1.1 kB
87	
88	The entire runtime — lazy ref-getters, method binding, inheritance/`super`
89	resolution, teardown, `$watch`/`$watchEffect`, **and the full
90	hot-reload-for-classes engine** — ships as **1.1 kB gzipped** (ES build).
91	The HMR machinery costs production literally zero bytes: every call site is
92	gated on the statically-replaceable `import.meta.env.DEV`, so bundlers
93	dead-code-eliminate all of it — verified by grepping the built output, not
94	assumed. Dev gets class grafting; prod gets the same 1.1 kB it always had.
95	
96	## Reads cost a little more
97	
98	State lives behind a getter. Each `this.x.value` does a small indirection
99	before reaching the ref: a `toRaw` call and a cache lookup. A native
100	composable reads its closure ref directly.
101	
102	On a hot loop dominated by reads, with identical bodies:
103	
104	| 10M method calls         | time    | per call |
105	| ------------------------ | ------- | -------- |
106	| native composable `fn()` | ~48 ms  | ~4.8 ns  |
107	| ivue `inst.method()`     | ~240 ms | ~24 ns   |
108	
109	A method that hammers reactive state costs ~5× more per call than a native
110	closure. **Method dispatch is not the cost.** The getter-indirected reads
111	inside the method are.
112	
113	In absolute terms, 24 ns is nothing. It only matters when you call something
114	millions of times.
115	
116	## The template boundary
117	
118	The standard is the raw instance — templates read Refs/Computeds as `.value` at the
119	raw column's cost. Wrapper costs shown for comparison; both wrappers were
120	retired ([Components & Templates](/guide/components)). Measured per read:
121	
122	| access path          | **raw (the standard)** | shallow unwrap proxy | `reactive()` |
123	| -------------------- | ---------------------- | -------------------- | ------------ |
124	| plain derived getter | **13.7 ns**            | 24.3 ns              | 75.4 ns      |
125	| ref-getter           | **4.1 ns**             | 22.6 ns              | 59.5 ns      |
126	| method               | **4.0 ns**             | 22.1 ns              | 60.3 ns      |
127	
128	Raw access pays 4–14 ns — no proxy on the path at all. Class internals and
129	templates run at the same column. The wrapper columns exist only as the
130	receipts for why they lost — a `proxyRefs`-style shallow view costs ~2–5×,
131	`reactive()` ~6–15×.
132	
133	## Hot loops
134	
135	When you do have such a loop, hoist the refs out of the getters once:
136	
137	```ts
138	calculate() {
139	  const w = this.w, h = this.h        // hoist: one getter access each
140	  let s = 0
141	  for (let i = 0; i < 1e7; i++) {
142	    s += Math.sqrt(w.value ** 2 + h.value ** 2)   // direct ref reads now
143	  }
144	  return s
145	}
146	```
147	
148	The inner loop now reads refs directly and runs at native speed.
149	
150	## The mental model
151	
152	- **ivue**: cheap to create, light in memory, slightly costlier to read.
153	- **ivue v1 (unreleased) / native composable**: costlier to create, heavier per instance, cheap to read.
154	
155	Pick by workload. Most apps create and render far more than they hot-loop, so
156	ivue's creation win usually dominates. Where it doesn't, the read cost is
157	erasable.

the prototype — testable, hot-graftable, minimum footprint. See
[Computed & Watch](/guide/computed-watch#computed-your-usememo).

Full write-up, machine notes, honest-cost accounting and caveats:
[`demo/formula/RESULTS.md`](https://github.com/infinite-system/ivue/blob/main/demo/formula/RESULTS.md).

```bash
# from the ivue repo root — the interactive playground
npx vite demo --host --port 5182     # then open /grid-formula
node demo/formula/measure.mjs http://localhost:5182         # 100k protocol
node demo/formula/measure.mjs http://localhost:5182 25000   # 1M cells
```

## The flyweight grid: 20 million cells

The grids above price the cell **instance**. The flyweight sketch
(`sketch/flyweight-grid/`, working and measured, structural proofs run at
full scale) removes even that: ground truth lives in columnar typed arrays,
cell objects are disposable three-field facades created per render, and
reactivity is a sparse overlay that materializes per observation. One law
governs all of it:

> **Everything costs proportional to what's observed; nothing costs
> proportional to what exists.**

**20 columns × 1,000,000 rows = 20,000,000 live cells**, ~55% real
Excel-syntax formulas, same parser, same gc-forced 3-run protocol:

| Metric                              | measured (production build) |
| ----------------------------------- | --------------------------: |
| Model creation, 20,000,000 cells    |                  **67.1 ms** |
| Model heap                          |                 **89.48 MB** |
| **Bytes per cell**                  |                   **4.7 B** |
| After 30 viewports across 1M rows   |        +0.3 MB of overlay   |
| Full-column `SUM(A1:A1000000)`      |    live, 245 block edges    |

That last pair is the architecture: memory is **O(viewport), not
O(rows-ever-visited)** — viewport-tied eviction returns scrolled-away
overlay to the collector, and released cells re-materialize correctly on
re-observation. A write to a cell nobody is observing allocates nothing and
notifies no one. And because behavior lives on prototypes, the formula
engine was **hot-swapped under the live 20M-cell model** — edited on disk,
grafted by [class HMR](/guide/hmr), totals recomputed through the new
engine, zero state loss. A compiled/WASM engine cannot do that at any
price: its code and its memory die together.

### The per-cell cost ladder

Every rung measured, same machine family, same protocol:

| a live cell, at rest                 | bytes/cell | what the cell is             |
| ------------------------------------ | ---------: | ---------------------------- |
| composable (idiomatic Vue)           |       ~758 | closures + eager ref/computeds |
| ivue instance grid (formula)         |        ~67 | plain object + lazy overlay  |
| plain POJO (no reactivity at all)    |        ~40 | `{ row, col, raw }`          |
| **ivue flyweight columnar**          |    **4.7** | 1 B kind + 8 B Float64, shared |

The flyweight sits **8.5× below the "theoretical floor"** — because the
floor was never plain objects; it was ground truth. A cell at rest is one
byte of kind tag plus eight bytes of number, and it is still fully
reactive, formula-capable and editable the moment anything observes it.
For scale: Google Sheets caps at 10M cells — this 20M-cell document cannot
be created there (architectural comparison, not a benchmark).

Status, honestly: a **sketch** — measured, verified in the DOM down to row
1,000,000, its structural suite green at real scale, but not yet packaged
as a shipping layer. The full material lives in the repo:
[`RESULTS.md`](https://github.com/infinite-system/ivue/blob/main/sketch/flyweight-grid/RESULTS.md)
(measurements, the steady-state memory ceiling, the hot-swap demo),
[`DESIGN.md`](https://github.com/infinite-system/ivue/blob/main/sketch/flyweight-grid/DESIGN.md)
(mechanisms, including the discovered O(n²) parser-aggregation finding and
the columnar fast path), and
[`Flyweight.invariants.md`](https://github.com/infinite-system/ivue/blob/main/sketch/flyweight-grid/Flyweight.invariants.md)
(the structural spec and its impossibility boundary).

```bash
# standalone demo, from the ivue repo root
npx vite sketch/flyweight-grid --host
node sketch/flyweight-grid/measure.mjs <url>
```

## Methodology
